options.name: Xavier Becerra
options.about: Former US Health and Human Services secretary and California attorney general.

options.name: Steve Hilton
options.about: Former Fox News host, Trump-aligned; ran on cost of living and rolling back regulation.

sides.a: Becerra: continuity on healthcare expansion, housing bonds, and climate rules; deep federal experience.
sides.b: Hilton: cut taxes and regulation, argues one-party rule made California unaffordable.

options.name: Fiona Ma
options.about: State Treasurer since 2019.

options.name: Gloria Romero
options.about: Former Democratic state senator who switched parties; school choice advocate.

sides.a: Ma: two terms managing the state's bonds and the housing-loan program she championed in Prop 37.
sides.b: Romero: education reform, breaks with the Democratic establishment she came from.

sos.title: Secretary of State

options.name: Shirley N. Weber
options.about: Incumbent; expanded vote-by-mail and automatic registration.

options.name: Don Wagner
options.about: Orange County supervisor; backs voter ID and tighter roll maintenance.

sides.a: Weber: keep universal mail ballots, same-day registration, and the current certification process.
sides.b: Wagner: voter ID, more frequent roll purges, says trust in elections needs tighter rules.

options.name: Malia M. Cohen
options.about: Incumbent; former Board of Equalization chair.

options.name: Herb Morgan
options.about: Businessman; campaigned on audits of state spending.

sides.a: Cohen: continuity; audits focused on local governments and unclaimed property.
sides.b: Morgan: more aggressive audits of state agencies, pitched as a fiscal watchdog.

options.name: Eleni Kounalakis
options.about: Term-limited lieutenant governor; former ambassador.

options.name: Jennifer Hawks
options.about: Financial advisor; ran on debt reduction.

sides.a: Kounalakis: keep issuing the housing and school bonds voters approve.
sides.b: Hawks: slow bond issuance, argues the state carries too much debt.

options.name: Rob Bonta
options.about: Incumbent; sued the federal government repeatedly on immigration and environment.

options.name: Michael Gates
options.about: Former Huntington Beach city attorney; fought the state on housing and sanctuary rules.

sides.a: Bonta: enforcement on polluters, gun laws, and corporate consumer cases; litigation against federal rollbacks.
sides.b: Gates: local control, public safety emphasis, less litigation against Washington.

insurance.title: Insurance Commissioner

options.name: Jane Kim
options.about: Former SF supervisor; wants a public option for wildfire and disaster insurance.

options.name: Ben Allen
options.about: State senator; the party's pick, authored climate disclosure laws.

sides.a: Kim: public disaster insurance, harder line on insurers leaving the state.
sides.b: Allen: work with insurers to keep them in the market, build on the Sustainable Insurance Strategy.

options.name: Tom Umberg
options.about: State senator from Orange County.

options.name: Denis Bilodeau
options.about: Runs a taxpayer association; Orange County water district director.

sides.a: Umberg: keep the board focused on fair assessments and taxpayer service.
sides.b: Bilodeau: taxpayer-advocate framing, wants the board to push back on assessments.

options.name: Scott Peters
options.about: Incumbent since 2013; moderate, climate and housing focus.

options.name: Steve Cohen
options.about: Businessman; border and cost-of-living campaign.

sides.a: Peters: seniority on energy and climate committees, votes with Democrats on most things.
sides.b: Cohen: border enforcement, spending cuts.

options.name: Tasha Boerner
options.about: Incumbent; coastal access and housing bills.

options.name: Trinity Hannaway
options.about: Self-described taxpayer advocate.

sides.a: Boerner: coastal protection, transit, and the Assembly's housing package.
sides.b: Hannaway: lower taxes and fees, less state mandate on cities.

judges.title: Supreme Court and Court of Appeal justices

options.name: Retain all 18
options.about: Retention votes on sitting justices, most appointed by Newsom or Brown. None has a public discipline record and no group campaigned against any of them.

options.name: Vote no on some
options.about: Nobody organized a no campaign this cycle. A no vote on a specific justice needs a specific reason.

sides.a: Yes: the default for justices with clean records; every Supreme Court retention since 1986 has passed.
sides.b: No: used when a justice has a discipline record or an organized campaign cites specific rulings. Not the case here.

options.name: Richard Barrera
options.about: San Diego Unified board member and labor organizer.

options.name: Sonja Shaw
options.about: Chino Valley school board president behind the parental-notification fights.

sides.a: Barrera: fund schools, defend the state curriculum, union-aligned.
sides.b: Shaw: parental rights, notification policies, school choice.

p1.title: Prop 1
p1.what: $11.25B in bonds for affordable rental housing, homelessness programs, and veterans' housing.

sides.a: Yes: the state's largest housing commitment in years; Habitat, teachers, and veterans' groups for.
sides.b: No: adds debt service to the general fund; critics say bonds build slowly and expensively.

p2.title: Prop 2
p2.what: Doubles the cap on reserve deposits so the state can save more in good years.

sides.a: Yes: bigger reserves so services survive downturns without cuts.
sides.b: No: money parked in reserves is money not spent on current needs.

p3.title: Prop 3
p3.what: Keeps the top income tax rates on income over about $371k, which were set to expire, and sends the revenue mostly to K-12.

sides.a: Yes: teachers, nurses, Planned Parenthood; the tax funds schools and has been in place since 2012.
sides.b: No: Chamber and Jarvis argue it pushes high earners out and should sunset as promised.

p4.title: Prop 4
p4.what: Lets the state and local governments offer public matching funds to candidates.

sides.a: Yes: less dependence on big donors; cities like LA already do it.
sides.b: No: taxpayer money for politicians' ads; Jarvis against.

p5.title: Prop 5
p5.what: A recall election would be a remove-or-not vote only; the successor would be set by law instead of a same-ballot replacement contest.

sides.a: Yes: ends the 2003-style scenario where a replacement wins with a small plurality.
sides.b: No: voters lose the ability to pick the replacement directly.

p37.title: Prop 37
p37.what: $25B bond for shared-appreciation loans covering up to 17% of the price of homes under $1.5M, repaid by the buyers.

sides.a: Yes: access to ownership for people who can pay a mortgage but not a down payment; Treasurer Ma for.
sides.b: No: can leave buyers over-leveraged and lifts prices; DSA took no position, preferring the state build rentals.

p38.title: Prop 38
p38.what: $8.4B in bonds for immunology research, with a large share directed to a single nonprofit institute.

sides.a: Yes: a research investment on the model of the stem-cell bond.
sides.b: No: half the money goes to one nonprofit tied to the billionaire sponsor; unusual structure.

p39.title: Prop 39
p39.short: Voter ID and proof of citizenship
p39.what: Requires photo ID to vote and documentary proof of citizenship to register.

sides.a: Yes: supporters say it builds confidence in elections.
sides.b: No: suppresses low-income, elderly, and immigrant voters; ACLU and League of Women Voters against.

p40.title: Prop 40
p40.what: One-time 5% tax on net worth over $1B, revenue to healthcare and schools.

sides.a: Yes: Bernie Sanders and SEIU-UHW; fewer than 200 households pay it.
sides.b: No: capital flight and valuation fights; Newsom and the Chamber opposed.

p41.title: Prop 41
p41.what: Audit and spending-limit rules written so that if it gets more votes than Prop 40, Prop 40 is nullified.

sides.a: Yes: framed as accountability for new taxes.
sides.b: No: exists to cancel Prop 40.

p42.title: Prop 42
p42.what: Bans taxes on personal property and wealth, retroactive to January 1; a second counter to Prop 40.

sides.a: Yes: a permanent block on wealth taxes.
sides.b: No: a poison pill that ties the state's hands on future revenue.

p43.title: Prop 43
p43.what: Raises the threshold for local citizen-initiated special taxes from a majority to two-thirds.

sides.a: Yes: Jarvis says a supermajority protects taxpayers.
sides.b: No: minority rule over local funding; nurses and firefighters against.

p44.title: Prop 44
p44.what: Requires community clinics to spend 90% of revenue on direct patient care.

sides.a: Yes: SEIU-UHW says it stops clinic chains from hoarding reserves and overpaying executives.
sides.b: No: the Democratic Party and clinic associations say it adds burden during federal cuts and could close clinics.

p45.title: Prop 45
p45.what: Lets projects labeled essential skip environmental review.

sides.a: Yes: faster housing and infrastructure; CEQA lawsuits delay projects for years.
sides.b: No: 'essential' is broad, and it removes the public's main tool against bad projects.

mA.title: Measure A
mA.what: Creates an ethics commission, an independent auditor, and a budget analyst; supervisor term limits go from 8 to 12 years.

sides.a: Yes: oversight the county has never had.
sides.b: No: longer term limits for the supervisors who wrote it.

mA.search: San Diego County Measure A 2026 charter

mB.title: Measure B
mB.what: Half-cent countywide sales tax, up to $450M a year for healthcare, childcare, Tijuana River cleanup, and public safety. No sunset.

sides.a: Yes: backfills federal cuts; DSA and SanDiego350 say yes despite the regressive mechanism.
sides.b: No: a regressive tax with no end date; Jarvis against.

mB.search: San Diego County Measure B 2026 sales tax

mM.title: Measure M
mM.what: $3.5B bond for repairs and classrooms, with a union labor agreement. Needs 55%.

sides.a: Yes: aging campuses, and the district has passed every bond since 2008.
sides.b: No: property-tax add-on on top of earlier bonds still being repaid.
